author: Wagner
title: The end foretold
where: *Götterdämmerung*, the Prelude and Act 3, with the English of Margaret Armour (1911)
about: *Götterdämmerung* is the last of the four operas of Wagner’s *Ring of the Nibelung*; he wrote the words himself. In the Prelude the three Norns, the Fates, sing as they pass a golden rope, and the third foretells the burning of Valhalla, the hall of the gods. In Act 3 the Rhinemaidens tell Siegfried he will be killed that day unless he gives them the ring; he refuses, and they pass judgment on him. At the end Brünnhilde, at his pyre, sends Wotan’s ravens home and throws the torch.

view.says: Auden told the English Institute in 1940 that the people of the *Ring* behave oddly: their mistakes are ones they know in advance to be mistakes. The audience of *Oedipus Rex* knows what its hero does not; here the actors know as well. His example is Valhalla, set on fire with wood of the World Ash Tree; he asks why Wotan keeps such fuel there.
view.quote: the actors are never tired of explaining exactly what is going to happen and how awful it will be; they deny their own knowledge
view.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 81–82

plates.heading: The third Norn foretells the end
plates.label: Wagner

lenses.label: Stave

threads.sound: of a vowel that opens the word

lenses.caption: These lines do not rhyme. The colored letters are staves, or alliteration: one sound at the head of stressed words, the binding of the oldest German verse. Wagner wrote in 1851 that end-rhyme was a cheat and that this verse bends to the accents of speech. Auden, in 1944, called the words of the Ring alliterative verse full of old and embarrassing expressions; sehrend, wounding, is a word that written German lost early. After the first, the lines pair off: br and h, s and gl, then vowels, which count as alike. Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins: here ewigen, eternal, and Ende, end.
lenses.why: Wagner gave up end-rhyme for the stave of the oldest German verse because, he wrote, it follows the accents of speech and makes one image of the words it joins; here it joins eternal to end.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. What a stave is: Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, under *Stabreim*, and Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5. Wagner’s reasons: *A Communication to My Friends* (1851), in W. Ashton Ellis’s translation, pp. 375–76, and *Opera and Drama* (1851), p. 227. Auden on the meter: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 503. *Sehren*, *ewig* and *Ende*: Grimm.

lenses.label: Dawn

notes.note: The ash from which Wotan cut his spear; the second Norn has just told how he had it felled.
Grimm’s dictionary defines the word as the everlasting, the endless; Armour has *high*.
The phrase is sung twice in the libretto: here, and by Brünnhilde in the third passage.

lenses.caption: The opera’s title is never sung in it. Its two halves stand here: Götter, gods, and dämmert. Dämmerung is the half-light of morning or evening, and the title word, on record from 1772, came from confusing two Old Norse names, the fate of the gods and their darkening. With auf, up, the Norn’s verb means to dawn: the end of the eternal gods dawns. Armour keeps the dawn and adds in darkness. The scene’s second line asks, in this verb, whether day is dawning; the answer is that the light is fire. Here too the dawn comes with fire: Valhalla burning with wood of the World Ash, which is Auden’s example.
lenses.why: The Norn foretells the end in the two halves of the title, with a verb that means to dawn; her dawn comes with the fire of the world-ash logs, which is Auden’s example of people who know what is coming.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, under *Götterdämmerung*, *Dämmerung*, *aufdämmern* and *ewig*. A search of the German libretto for the title word. The [first lines of the Prelude](#/read/gotterdammerung/prelude:2), where the second Norn asks whether day is dawning and the third answers that the light is fire. Auden’s example: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 82.

lenses.label: Against
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: The Rhinemaidens sum Siegfried up four times, each in two halves: something to his credit, then what stands against it. He thinks himself wise and strong, and is bound and blind. The two middle sentences match, three words then four, both closing on sie nicht, them not: oaths he swore and does not heed, runes he knows and does not read. A highest good was given him, and he does not know he threw it away. Auden says the people of the Ring deny their own knowledge.
lenses.why: Four times the verdict sets something to Siegfried’s credit beside what stands against it; the third says he knows runes and does not read them, and Auden’s charge against the Ring’s people is that they deny their own knowledge.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. Antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 82.

lenses.label: Knowing

notes.note: German *weise* and *weiß*, knows, come from one root, which meant to see: to know was to have seen.
Grimm gives the verb as to suppose or assume, found in written German only in older times, and its simple form *wähnen* as to believe, or to assume falsely.
Grimm: a secret, a secret counsel, a character of the Germanic secret and magic writing; in the Prelude Brünnhilde says she has given him her holy runes.
The same word as English *read*, whose old senses were to counsel and to interpret; at his death Hagen asks him, in a form of this verb, whether he can make out the ravens’ whisper.
*Rede* is an old spelling of *read* that poets fond of old words kept in use; Wagner’s line has *does not* where Armour has *cannot*.

lenses.caption: Words of knowing run through the verdict. Two of them, weise, wise, and weiß, knows, come from one root, which meant to see; the man who thinks himself wise is called blind. Runen are secrets, and letters of a secret script; Brünnhilde gave him hers. The verb rät, the same word as English read, means to counsel, interpret or guess. Wagner’s line says he does not read them; Armour’s cannot is her own. Auden says the people of the Ring explain exactly what is coming and deny their own knowledge. Here the same voices have just told Siegfried he will be killed today, and he keeps the ring.
lenses.why: The verdict is made of words for knowing; its third sentence says he knows runes and does not read them, just after he was told he would die today, and Auden says the Ring’s people deny their own knowledge.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Online Etymology Dictionary under *wise*, *wit*, *read* and *rede*; Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch* under *Rune*, *raten*, *verwähnen* and *wähnen*. Brünnhilde’s runes: [the Prelude](#/read/gotterdammerung/prelude:51). The warning and his answer: [Act 3](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-3:82). Hagen’s question: [Act 3](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-3:213), with the German of the line. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 82.

lenses.label: English

threads.sound: of a vowel that opens the word

lenses.caption: The colored letters are staves, Wagner’s in the German and Armour’s in the English. In his second and third sentences the stave ties what Siegfried has to what he fails to do with it: Eide, oaths, to achtet, heeds, and Runen to rät. In this verse vowels count as alike. Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins. Armour keeps three of his staves on the same letter: blind and bound, Runes and rede, glorious gift. Two of these are the same words in both languages. The oldest English verse was bound this way too. She drops his w, which opens and closes the passage, and his vowels, and adds an f of her own.
lenses.why: In the two matched sentences Wagner’s stave ties what Siegfried has to what he fails to do with it; Armour keeps three of his staves on the same letter, twice with the same words, and drops two.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Wagner on what a stave does, and on vowels: *Opera and Drama* (1851), in W. Ashton Ellis’s translation, p. 227. The words the two languages share: the Online Etymology Dictionary under *blind*, *bind*, *rune*, *read* and *rede*. Alliteration in the oldest English verse: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5.

lenses.label: Now

notes.note: Grimm derives the verb from the noun *rune*, a secret. In Act 1 Waltraute uses it for the wish Wotan whispered, that the ring go back to the Rhine’s daughters, and Brünnhilde uses it when she sends her refusal to the gods.
The verb that means to dawn, completed by *auf* at the end of the line, as in the first passage.
The Norn’s line has *ewig da* in this place: forever, then.
The Norn’s words were *den wirft der Gott*, the god throws it.
The Norn’s word for the fire the god was to throw; Grimm gives it as a burning piece of wood, and English *brand* is the same word.

lenses.caption: Brünnhilde’s sentence is the third Norn’s, come true. Götter Ende, the gods’ end, is sung twice in the libretto, there and here, each time with dämmert and auf, dawns. The Norn’s gods were eternal, and their end was to dawn then, da, and forever, ewig. Here the gods are not called eternal, and the word is nun, now. The Norn said the god would throw the fire among the logs; Brünnhilde says werf ich, I throw. She sends Wotan’s ravens home to whisper it, Raunt, Waltraute’s verb in Act 1 for the wish he whispered. Auden observes that she and Siegfried make no new world: they burn with the old one.
lenses.why: The end comes in the words that foretold it, with now where the Norn sang then and forever, and I where she sang the god; Auden notes that the lovers make no new world and burn with the old one.
lenses.stands: The marks on this passage and on the first. A count of the phrase and of the verb in the German libretto. The third Norn’s [second prophecy](#/read/gotterdammerung/prelude:28) and [Waltraute’s account](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-1:290) of Wotan, each with its German. Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch* under *da*, *raunen* and *Brand*. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 81.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: *Rhein* and *Rhine*, like *Raben* and *ravens* two lines earlier, are the same words, so Wagner’s stave on *r* crosses into English.
*Whisper* becomes *tell*. In Act 1 Armour’s Waltraute says *whispered*.
*End*. For this word Armour wrote *downfall* in the Prelude and writes *doom* here.
*Dawns now*. In the Prelude she kept *Dawn*; here the gods are *drawing near*, so in her English the verb does not come back.
*I throw* becomes *thrown be*, with no *I*. In the Prelude her Norn says *is thrown*, with no god.

lenses.caption: Armour stays close, and where the two languages share a word she keeps the stave: ravens and Rhine for Raben and Rhein. Raunt, whisper, becomes Tell. Her English hardly shows that the Norn’s sentence returns. For the same German words she wrote downfall and Dawn in the Prelude and writes doom and drawing near here, so of that sentence only Gods and a stave on d come back. In both places her English names no thrower: is thrown there and thrown be here. Wagner names one each time: the god, then ich, I.
lenses.why: The English keeps Wagner’s stave where it shares his words, but it turns the returning sentence two ways and names no thrower, so the Norn’s prophecy does not come back in Brünnhilde’s mouth as it does in the German.
lenses.stands: The marks on this passage and on the first. Armour’s [third Norn](#/read/gotterdammerung/prelude:28) and her [Waltraute](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-1:290), each set against the German of the same lines. The Online Etymology Dictionary under *raven* and *Rhine*.

lenses.label: Told
lenses.what: where in the libretto each end is told before it comes

told.says: when the logs of the world-ash burn, the end of the gods will dawn
the fire will be thrown among the logs
Wotan has had the world-ash felled and its logs heaped round the hall, and sits there in silence
she will keep the ring, though the glory of Valhalla perish
Wotan and all the gods are waiting for their downfall

comes.what: throws the torch; in the last stage direction flames take the hall of the gods

told.says: through him Siegfried is already speeding to his doom
if Brünnhilde’s charge is true, let the point of Hagen’s spear be the one that strikes him dead
on the same spear-point, may its sharpness kill him
told by Brünnhilde that only Siegfried’s back can be wounded, he says his spear will strike there
tomorrow, on the hunt; it will be given out that a boar killed him
he will fall today unless he gives the ring to the Rhine
he tells the hunters that he was told he would be killed today

comes.what: drives his spear into Siegfried’s back, in a stage direction after this line

lenses.caption: The line down the page is the libretto: 2,026 lines of verse in this translation. Each mark is a place where someone speaks of the gods’ end or of Siegfried’s death before it comes: that it will come, or how. The earliest is the third Norn’s, at line 79. Siegfried names the weapon himself, in the oath on Hagen’s spear that Auden, in talk a friend wrote down, called wonderful. The Rhinemaidens tell him the day, and he repeats it to the hunters. Auden says these people never tire of explaining what will happen and how terrible it will be. The spear strikes after line 1,791; the torch is thrown at line 2,002.
lenses.why: Both ends are told again and again, by different voices, before they come, and Siegfried’s by Siegfried himself; Auden’s complaint is that the people of the Ring never tire of explaining what will happen.
lenses.stands: A count of the lines of verse in the text printed here; which lines count as tellings is a judgment. The oath: [Act 2](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-2:276). The warning: [Act 3](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-3:82). The spear: [Act 3](#/read/gotterdammerung/act-3:214). Auden on the oath: Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, p. 16. Auden on explaining: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 82.

auden.says: In the lecture of 1940 Auden tries two readings of the *Ring* as allegory and finds that each goes vague in this opera. To a historian it is the Germany of Wagner’s century: the gods are the old nobility, the dwarfs the men of money, the giants the workers, and Siegfried and Brünnhilde the pair who set the country free; yet at the end the ring only returns to the Rhine. On a psychoanalytic reading one would expect the pair to grow up and marry elsewhere, she Gunther and he Gutrune; the libretto shows those marriages as unfaithfulness that magic has worked, and fatal to both.
auden.quote: Siegfried and Brünnhilde do not create the new world, they go up in flames with the old
auden.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 81–82

auden.says: Auden took Wagner for the test case of his lecture because he thought him the greatest modern artist and the most typical. The story and its people are allegory, he says, yet Wagner treats them as realistically as opera can, turning recitative, sung speech, into an unending melody that follows the speaking voice. His explanation of the characters’ illogic is the composer: suffering was what Wagner’s art could express, and they act against sense so that he can keep writing the music he did best. For expressing failure, betrayed love like Brünnhilde’s included, Auden ranks him with the greatest geniuses. The best of him, he says, is in the monologues.
auden.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 80–81 and 83

auden.says: *New Year Letter*, the long poem Auden published in 1941, says that the hero Wagner put on the stage has done all his thinking once he knows that his ruin is fated, and lives to suffer. The note to those lines makes the same charge as the lecture. No Romantic artist is greater than Wagner, it says, because none goes further in the Romantic heresy of setting the necessity of cause above the necessity of logic. The operas are masterly case histories of people in trouble and, as plots, absurd: the fire at Valhalla, fed with wood of the World Ash, is the instance here too.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (1941), lines 1432 ff., p. 66, and the note to line 1432, pp. 143–44

auden.says: In 1944 Auden wrote notes for a college radio broadcast of *Die Walküre*, the second opera of the cycle. He says there that Wagner’s text for the *Ring*, dated by him to 1853, is in an alliterative meter full of old and embarrassing expressions.
auden.source: Program notes for a broadcast of *Die Walküre* (1944), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 503

auden.says: Alan Ansen, a friend who wrote down Auden’s conversation between 1946 and 1948, has him say that just three Wagner operas please him from beginning to end: *Die Walküre*, *Götterdämmerung* and *Tristan*. Within the *Ring* he puts this one second, after *Die Walküre*, and he names two things in it: the oath on the spear in Act 2, which he calls wonderful, and the duet of Brünnhilde and Waltraute in Act 1.
auden.source: Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, edited by Nicholas Jenkins (1991), p. 16

auden.says: In a BBC talk of 1955 on Tolkien, Auden sets Wagner’s ring beside Tolkien’s. The allegory of the *Ring*, he says first, is only political and psychological: Wotan is no true god, just an old feudal lord, no wiser and no better behaved than anyone else. Each ring gives its wearer rule over the world, and each can be made only by someone who gives up love. Wagner’s ring, because of Alberich’s curse, brings bad luck on every owner, yet it leaves them uncorrupted. Siegfried himself, although the woodbird has told him what it is, takes no interest in it and comes close to handing it back to the Rhinemaidens.
auden.source: “History, Feigned and Real” (BBC talk, 1955), in *Prose*, vol. III (2008), pp. 689–90

auden.says: Nietzsche’s *The Case of Wagner* was on the list of critical reading Auden recommended for the Michigan course, and the lecture of 1940 quotes it twice. In *The Dyer’s Hand* he says Nietzsche’s book first opened his ears to Wagner, and rates it above any other critical study of one figure he knows: an attack that never lets the reader forget how great its subject is. Elsewhere in *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden is mostly against opera sung in translation, because a listener hears syllables and not words. Wagner in English is unbearable to hear, he says, however good the translation: the new syllables do not fit the notes.
auden.source: *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 48 and 473; Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), p. 27

auden.says: Reviewing a life of Wagner in 1969, Auden sets out the theory of Wagner’s *Opera and Drama* (1851): the words matter as much as the music, or more; nobody sings together with anybody else; no word is said twice; regular meter is to be left alone, and rhyme too. Only *Das Rheingold* and Acts 1 and 2 of *Die Walküre*, he says, keep its rules. *Götterdämmerung* has, in a phrase he quotes, poisoned drinks, an ensemble of plotters and a massed chorus, and Bernard Shaw, he says, was right that it shares a good deal with Verdi’s *Un ballo in maschera*.
auden.source: “The Greatest of the Monsters,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 251–52

W. H. Auden, *New Year Letter* (1941), Part III, lines 1432 and after (p. 66), and the note to line 1432, pp. 143–44.

caveats: The German printed here is the text as sung. The poem Wagner printed in 1872, which Armour’s English appears to follow, words the first three lines of the second passage a little differently, with *strong* before *wise*, and has another word for *once* in the first.

Auden’s lecture of 1940, his radio notes of 1944, his talk of 1955, the verse and note of *New Year Letter*, Ansen’s *Table Talk* and Miller’s memoir were read only in snippets of scanned copies, a sentence at a time, and not in a full copy.
The praise of the oath on the spear comes from a friend’s record of Auden’s talk, not from Auden’s own text.
Which lines count as telling an end beforehand is a judgment. The drawing marks places where a character says that the end will come, or how; other lines only hint at it or call for it.
A stave is a matter of the ear. In the first line of the first passage *Weltesche* can be heard to bind with *war*, and that is left unmarked.
